correctness.rationale: For every palindrome embedding, termwise minima of each left and reflected partner form a strictly increasing left-half embedding. Reflection moves any off-axis center to the left, giving exactly the stated necessary-and-sufficient half-word conditions. Reverse completion proves sufficiency. Unique output parity and centers prove disjointness. The verified program compared the full output languages, all length coefficients, and totals for 2,713 exhaustive half-word choices, 11,962 host cases.

evidence: Hasan et al. (2013), Definition 1 and Algorithm 1, represent all palindromic subsequences of arbitrary strings; this is broader algorithmic input scope.
Holub–Saari, Theorem 2, prove a binary input-reconstruction theorem from the full set of scattered palindromes, rather than a graded counting identity.
broader_coverage.reasoning: An arbitrary-host generator can enumerate spectra for palindrome inputs but does not itself state the exact two-polynomial reflection law; it is broader in decision/generation scope but not a closed-form resolution of the proposed parameterized counting question. The reflection theorem narrows hosts while strengthening the explicit algebraic and output-language description. Residual risk is that this is a direct, unrecorded specialization of automaton results.

evidence: The 2021 result bounds any word with two copies of each symbol and evaluates the mirror of a permutation half; its special-case value agrees with twice the number of nonempty half subsequences.

The 2013 algorithm is mathematically capable of producing all palindromic outputs for a given host but requires constructing the full automaton; it does not assert the two displayed universal reflection polynomial identities.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The 2021 bounds imply the identity only for the distinct-letter mirror extremizer, not for arbitrary repetitions and center positions. The generic 2013 PSA implies computability of this output language, and its weights strongly suggest the reflection argument, but the explicit parametric equality and central correction are additional statements rather than a previously stated complete classification. This distinction may not survive all formulations of equivalence; it is a disclosed originality risk.

evidence: Mahalingam–Pandoh (2021), Proposition 5.1, gives the binomial count for a distinct-letter mirrored word, while §4–5 give general bounds.

Hasan et al. (2013), §2.1, use weighted automata to generate all palindromic subsequences of general hosts using matched halves; no specialized left-half generating-polynomial formula is stated in the inspected §2–3.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The theorem can be restated as a disjoint language bijection: for each nonempty subsequence of the left half there is one even and one off-axis-centered palindrome, and the optional central letter contributes a controlled extra layer. The generic palindromic-subsequence automaton is a substantive nearby mechanism that could yield these identities upon specialization; the explicit two parity cases and exact center correction were not located verbatim or as a stated corollary in the inspected material.

value.rationale: A complete all-length classification for every palindromic host on any finite alphabet, including arbitrary repeated letters and an exact odd-center correction. This resolves a natural family singled out by existing scattered-palindrome bounds, directly relates distinct output languages to elementary half-word subsequence polynomials, and avoids counting embeddings. The general language identities offer exact enumeration and a reusable representation, not a small ad hoc cutoff.
